Let \(\chi\) be the Legendre symbol on \(\mathbb F_p\), extended by \(\chi(0)=0\). We want the number \(N\) of \(x\) for which
\[
\chi(x-1)=\chi(x)=\chi(x+1)=1.
\]

For the moment consider
\[
J=\frac18\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}(1+\chi(x-1))(1+\chi(x))(1+\chi(x+1)).
\]
For \(x\notin\{-1,0,1\}\), the summand is exactly the indicator that \(x-1,x,x+1\) are all quadratic residues.

Expanding,
\[
8J=p+\sum_x\chi(x(x-1))+\sum_x\chi((x-1)(x+1))+\sum_x\chi(x(x+1))
+\sum_x\chi(x(x-1)(x+1)).
\]
Each nonconstant quadratic with nonzero discriminant contributes \(-1\), so
\[
8J=p-3+T,
\qquad
T:=\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}\chi(x^3-x).
\]

Now evaluate \(T\). Since \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), choose a quartic character \(\psi\) with \(\psi^2=\chi\) and \(\psi(x^2)=\chi(x)\). Then
\[
T=\sum_{x\ne0}\chi(x)\chi(x^2-1).
\]
Putting \(t=x^2\), the two square roots of \(t\) have the same Legendre symbol because \(\chi(-1)=1\), hence
\[
T=\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p}(1+\chi(t))\psi(t)\chi(1-t)
=J(\psi,\chi)+J(\psi^3,\chi),
\]
where \(J(\alpha,\beta)=\sum_t\alpha(t)\beta(1-t)\) is the Jacobi sum. The two terms are complex conjugates, so
\[
T=2\operatorname{Re}J(\psi,\chi).
\]

The standard quartic Jacobi-sum evaluation gives
\[
J(\psi,\chi)=a+bi,
\]
where \(p=a^2+b^2\), \(b\) is even, \(a\) is odd, and
\[
a\equiv-\left(\frac2p\right)\pmod4.
\]
By the definition of \(a\) in the problem, this is exactly the same \(a\). Therefore
\[
T=2a.
\]

So
\[
J=\frac{p-3+2a}{8}.
\]

It remains to remove the false contributions from \(x=-1,0,1\), where one of \(x-1,x,x+1\) is zero. Since \(\chi(-1)=1\) and \(\chi(2)=\varepsilon\),
\[
x=0 \text{ contributes } \frac12,
\]
while \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\) together contribute
\[
2\cdot \frac{1+\varepsilon}{4}=\frac{1+\varepsilon}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
N=\frac{p-3+2a}{8}-\frac12-\frac{1+\varepsilon}{2}
=\frac{p+2a-11-4\varepsilon}{8}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{p+2a-11-4\varepsilon}{8}}
\]
